story.headline: Oil fell about 1% on a report that US Vice President JD Vance wrote to Iran to restart peace talks. Today brings US growth and inflation figures at 7:30 AM CT and a European Central Bank decision.

reads.policy: Most central banks are still leaning toward higher rates because of energy-driven inflation. Markets eased their bets on a December Fed hike a little after chair Kevin Warsh refused to commit, which keeps the dollar steady rather than stronger. The European Central Bank today and the Bank of Japan overnight are both expected to wait until December.
reads.growth: The US economy still looks stronger than Europe's or Britain's, and that gap keeps favouring the dollar. Overnight surveys were mixed: Japanese households a little gloomier, New Zealand firms a little brighter. US third-quarter growth figures this morning are the next big check.
reads.inflation: Energy keeps prices high, which is why most central banks are still leaning toward hikes. There are early signs of relief: Australia's import costs fell as fuel shipping eased. The US inflation measure the Fed watches most comes this morning, and it will shape how sure markets are of a December Fed hike.
reads.risk: Asian shares slipped after a weak result from Google's owner, Alphabet, but there was no rush into safe currencies like the yen and franc. A report of US outreach to Iran eased war fears a little, while threats of strikes after next week's US elections keep the risk alive. Calm for now, but fragile.
reads.tot: Oil eased on hopes that the US and Iran might talk, but it is still far above pre-war levels. That keeps helping exporters like Canada and Australia and costing importers like Japan and the euro area. A real peace deal would shift that balance quickly.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and Canada's rate hike has not yet forced them to buy back. Their bets against the kiwi paid off after New Zealand's surprise hold. In the pound and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.
reads.fiscal: Chancellor John Healey's first UK Budget passed calmly, with borrowing set to fall, so UK bonds and the pound took it in stride. France's budget fight is still unresolved and keeps a weight on the euro; reporters are likely to raise it at the European Central Bank's press conference today.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28, but two officials voted to hike, and markets still see a December hike as likely. That keeps US rates high and gives the dollar a floor.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal, kept up by high energy prices, and the economy is still growing strongly.
fed.watch: The PCE inflation figures at 7:30 AM CT Thursday: a hot reading would make a December hike close to certain, a soft one would loosen it.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% on October 28, its first hike since 2023, and said more may be needed. That has narrowed the gap with US rates and helped the loonie.
boc.priced: December: another hike possible, about a coin toss.
boc.why: Higher energy prices have lifted Canadian inflation, and the bank raised its inflation forecasts sharply.
boc.watch: Deputy governor Nicolas Vincent speaks Thursday, and Canada's August growth figures come Friday; both shape the odds of a December hike.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by holding at 2.75% on October 28, but it says more tightening is likely. That makes December a live meeting and limits the kiwi's fall.
rbnz.priced: December: a hike possible; no firm odds yet.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the 1–3% target, and firms say they plan to raise prices more.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand job and price figures before the December 9 decision, and anything Governor Anna Breman says about timing.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank is expected to hold today and lean toward a hike in December, because inflation is at a three-year high. France's budget trouble is the main weight on the euro.
ecb.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Energy costs have pushed euro-area inflation well above the 2% goal, even as growth slows.
ecb.watch: The decision at 8:15 AM CT and President Christine Lagarde's press conference at about 8:45 AM CT: how clearly she signals December, and what she says about France.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on Friday and raise rates in December. Rates are still far below other major economies', which keeps the yen weak until they rise.
boj.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
boj.why: Inflation is broadening beyond energy, with the bank's own underlying gauge at a three-year high, which builds the case for a hike.
boj.watch: Tokyo consumer prices at 6:30 PM CT Thursday, then the decision and new forecasts during Friday in Japan (overnight Thursday CT). Any move by Tokyo to buy yen would also matter.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates on November 3 after inflation ran hotter than it forecast. That supports the Aussie.
rba.why: Underlying inflation is running above the bank's own forecasts, though cheaper imports point to some relief later.
rba.watch: Australian producer prices Thursday night CT, then the decision at 9:30 PM CT Monday, November 2.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, and the debate is already about December. The calm Budget removed one risk before the decision.
boe.priced: November: hike all but certain; December: a second hike possible.
boe.why: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, driven by energy and fuel, with service prices still sticky.
boe.watch: The decision on November 5 at 6:00 AM CT, and whether the bank hints at a second hike in December.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and has said it is less ready to fight a weaker franc. Swiss inflation is low, so the franc mostly moves on global fear and calm.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Inflation is below target, so the bank has no reason to raise rates while others do.
snb.watch: Board member Petra Tschudin speaks Thursday; the next decision is December 10.

USD.summary: The dollar sits near the top of the board because the Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates again and US inflation is running hot. Markets eased those hike bets a little after the Fed's October hold.

notes.policy: The Fed's next move still looks like a hike, likely in December, which keeps US rates high.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running well above the Fed's goal, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: growth is slowing, energy imports cost more, and France's budget fight weighs on it. Inflation is high, so the European Central Bank still leans toward a hike in December.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank is expected to wait until December, so it lags banks that are moving sooner.
notes.growth: Euro-area business surveys missed forecasts in October, with France back in decline.
notes.inflation: Prices are still rising fast in the pipeline, which keeps pressure on the European Central Bank to hike.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so high oil drains money out.
notes.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: France's unresolved budget and heavy debt keep investors wary of euro-area bonds.

GBP.summary: The pound scores well because the Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates in November, inflation is high and the economy is holding up. The calm Budget removed one risk.

notes.policy: The Bank of England is expected to raise rates on November 5, among the most likely hikes of any major bank.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been stronger than expected, even though shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, which keeps the Bank of England leaning toward hikes.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below other major economies' and high oil costs Japan money. It gets some support when markets turn nervous.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan is expected to wait until December to raise rates, keeping a wide gap with US rates.
notes.risk: The yen tends to gain when investors look for safety, and Tokyo's warnings about intervention limit how weak it gets.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates, but the franc still draws money when markets get nervous.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is below target, which keeps the Swiss National Bank from raising rates.
notes.risk: The franc tends to gain when investors look for safety, though lately the yen has led that move.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well because the Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates in November and high commodity prices bring money in. A weakening job market is the main drag.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates on November 3, which supports the Aussie.
notes.growth: Business surveys slipped into decline in October and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying inflation ran hotter than the bank expected, which keeps hikes coming.
notes.tot: Australia sells energy and resources abroad, so high prices bring money into the country.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well now that the Bank of Canada has started raising rates and high oil prices bring money in. Growth is the soft spot.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and may do so again in December.
notes.growth: Canadian spending has been only modestly firm, which leaves growth the weak spot.
notes.inflation: Producer and raw-material prices are rising fast, which keeps the Bank of Canada leaning toward more hikes.
notes.tot: Canada is a big oil exporter, so high crude prices bring money into the country.

NZD.summary: The kiwi fell after New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike, but the bank still expects to tighten later. A steady economy and firm export prices limit the damage.

notes.growth: New Zealand's services sector keeps growing, and business confidence rose in October.
notes.risk: The kiwi tends to do well when markets are calm.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
